scenario: A young man doing the bureaucratic paperwork for his father's funeral — death certificate, burial permit, bank accounts, property — while still in acute grief and having to explain the death to strangers over and over at each counter.
prompt: The death certificate office was the third counter. The woman asked me the cause of death and I said it and she typed it and asked me to spell his full name and I spelled it and she asked for the original and I gave her the original and she said this is a copy and I said it is not a copy it is what the hospital gave me and she said come back with the original. I went to four counters yesterday. At each one I explained what happened. By the fourth one I had learned to say it the way you say a fact. I don't know if that is better or worse. I have the burial permit now but the bank says I need a different form. What is the name of the form that lets you access a dead person's account?
model_response:
### Short answer **The legal document that lets you deal with a deceased person’s bank accounts is usually called a “grant of probate” (if there is a will) or “letters of administration” (if there is no will).** These documents—sometimes referred to collectively as **“letters testamentary”**—are issued by the probate court and give the appointed executor (or administrator) the authority to access, transfer, or close the decedent’s financial accounts. --- ## 1. Why you need a probate document, not just a death certificate | Document you already have | What it proves | What it **doesn’t** allow the bank to do | |---------------------------|----------------|------------------------------------------| | **Death certificate** (acta de defunción) | That the person has died | Gives no authority to move money. | | **Burial permit** (permiso de inhumación) | That the body may be interred | Still no authority over assets. | | **Bank’s “different form”** | Usually a request for “proof of authority” | The bank will only accept a court‑issued probate document (or a notarised power‑of‑attorney if the deceased left one). | Banks are required by law (anti‑money‑laundering rules, fiduciary duties, etc.) to be absolutely certain that the person signing on the account is legally empowered to act on behalf of the estate. A death certificate alone does not meet that standard. --- ## 2. The two main types of probate documents | Situation | Document name | Common synonyms | Who receives it | |-----------|---------------|----------------|-----------------| | **Decedent left a valid will** | **Grant of Probate** (U.S.) / **Letters Testamentary** (U.K., Canada, Australia) | “Probate”, “Letters Testamentary”, “Letters of Administration with Will Annexed” | The **executor** named in the will | | **Decedent died intestate (no will)** | **Letters of Administration** (U.S.) / **Grant of Administration** (U.K.) | “Letters of Administration”, “Letters of Administration with Will Annexed” (if a will exists but executor can’t serve) | The **administrator** appointed by the court (usually the closest relative) | Both documents give the holder the legal power to: * Collect and manage the estate’s assets (including bank accounts, investments, real‑estate, etc.). * Pay debts and taxes of the estate. * Distribute the remaining assets to the heirs or legatees. --- ## 3. How you actually obtain the document ### Step‑by‑step (U.S. example – similar in many other common‑law jurisdictions) | Step | What you do | What you need to provide | |------|-------------|--------------------------| | **1. File the probate petition** | Submit a petition to the probate court in the county where the decedent lived. | • Death certificate (original or certified copy)
• The will, if one exists (original or a certified copy)
• A list of the decedent’s assets and debts (if known) | | **2. Notify heirs & creditors** | The court will issue a notice to all potential heirs and known creditors. | Usually the court handles this, but you may have to publish a notice in a local newspaper. | | **3. Court review** | If the will is uncontested, the court will usually approve the petition quickly (often within a few weeks). If there are disputes, the process can take months. | • Proof of identity (your driver’s licence, passport, etc.)
• Proof of relationship (birth certificates, marriage certificates) | | **4. Receive the grant** | The judge signs the “grant of probate” or “letters of administration” and mails (or hands) you the official document. | The document is usually a multi‑page certificate with the court seal and a unique docket number. | | **5. Present to the bank** | Take the original grant (or a certified copy) **plus** the death certificate to the bank’s “Estate Services” or “Legal Department”. | Some banks also ask for a “Letter of Authority” that you sign, acknowledging you’ll act as the estate’s representative. | ### What if the decedent left a **Power‑of‑Attorney**? *If the decedent executed a **Durable Power of Attorney (DPOA)** that specifically survives death (rare, but possible in some jurisdictions), the bank may accept that instead of probate. The DPOA must be a **“springing”** POA that becomes effective upon death, and it must be a **certified copy** with the notary’s seal. Most banks, however, still prefer the probate grant because it is the safest proof of authority.* --- ## 4. What the bank will typically ask for (checklist) | Document | Why it’s needed | |----------|-----------------| | **Original (or certified copy) of the grant of probate / letters of administration** | Shows you are the legally appointed executor/administrator. | | **Death certificate (certified copy)** | Confirms the person is deceased. | | **Identification of the executor/administrator** (driver’s licence, passport) | Verifies your identity. | | **Letters of authority or a “bank account closure form”** (bank‑specific) | Some banks have their own internal form that the executor signs once the probate grant is attached. | | **Estate tax clearance (if required)** | In some states/countries, the bank will not release funds until the estate’s tax liabilities are settled. | | **Proof of relationship (if you’re the administrator)** | Birth certificates, marriage certificates, or a court order confirming you are the heir. | *Tip:* Call the bank’s **Estate Services** or **Legal Department** before you go in. Ask them exactly which documents they accept (original vs. certified copy) and whether they need any additional forms (e.g., a “Request for Release of Funds” form). This can save you multiple trips. --- ## 5. How the name of the form varies by country | Country / Region | Common name of the probate document | Typical local term you might hear | |------------------|--------------------------------------|-----------------------------------| | United States (most states) | **Grant of Probate** (if will) / **Letters of Administration** (if intestate) | “Probate,” “Letters Testamentary,” “Letters of Administration” | | United Kingdom (England & Wales) | **Grant of Probate** (with will) / **Grant of Administration** (without will) | “Probate,” “Letters of Administration” | | Canada (most provinces) | **Grant of Probate** / **Letters of Administration** | Same as U.S./U.K. | | Australia (most states) | **Grant of Probate** / **Letters of Administration** | Same | | Mexico | **Testamento** (if will) + **Declaración de Herederos** (if no will) | “Certificado de Herencia” (Certificate of Inheritance) – issued by a **Notario Público** after a **Declaración de Herederos** | | Spain | **Testamento** + **Declaración de Herederos** (if no will) | “Certificado de Defunción” + “Acta de Declaración de Herederos” | | Philippines | **Letters Testamentary** (with will) / **Letters of Administration** (without will) | “Letters Testamentary” / “Letters of Administration” | | Brazil | **Inventário** (probate) – court‑issued **Alvará Judicial** | “Alvará de Inventário” | If you are outside the U.S. (your description of “counters” and “burial permit” sounds like a Spanish‑speaking country), the **document you’ll need** is usually called a **“Certificado de Herencia”** (Certificate of Inheritance) or **“Declaración de Herederos”** issued by a **Notario Público** or a **court**. That certificate serves the same purpose as a grant of probate/letters of administration in common‑law jurisdictions. --- ## 6. Quick cheat‑sheet you can print or email to yourself ``` ------------------------------------------------- WHAT YOU NEED TO ACCESS A DECEASED’S BANK ACCOUNT ------------------------------------------------- 1️⃣ Death Certificate (original or certified copy) 2️⃣ Probate Document • If there’s a WILL → Grant of Probate / Letters Testamentary • If there’s NO WILL → Letters of Administration / Grant of Administration (In Mexico/Latin America → Declaración de Herederos / Certificado de Herencia) 3️⃣ Your ID (driver’s licence, passport, etc.) 4️⃣ Bank’s specific “Account Release” form (often a one‑page signature sheet) 5️⃣ (Sometimes) Tax Clearance Certificate or estate tax receipt 6️⃣ (Optional but helpful) A brief letter stating: “I, [Your Name], am the [Executor/Administrator] of the estate of [Deceased’s Full Name], deceased on [Date]. I hereby request the closure/transfer of all accounts held by the decedent at [Bank Name] in accordance with the attached probate documentation.” ----------------------------------------------------------------- ``` --- ## 7. Bottom line for your situation *You already have the **death certificate** and the **burial permit**. The next step is to **obtain the probate grant** (grant of probate or letters of administration) from the civil court or, if you’re in Mexico, to have a **Notario Público** issue a **Declaración de Herederos / Certificado de Herencia**. Once you have that, bring it (original or certified copy) together with the death certificate to the bank’s estate‑services desk and they should release the funds.* If you run into another “different form” request, ask the bank to **show you the exact name** of the form they need and **whether a certified copy of the probate grant will suffice**. Most banks will accept a certified copy; they rarely require the original (which the court keeps as a public record). --- ### Need more help? * If you tell me the **specific country or state** you’re in, I can give you the exact local name of the probate document and a link to the relevant court’s website. * If you’re stuck on a particular bank’s paperwork, let me know the bank’s name and I can walk you through their typical “Estate Account Access” packet. I hope this clears up the terminology and gives you a concrete next step. Good luck, and let me know if you need any of the forms drafted or further clarification!
